---
title: "3.2.1. Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS)"
bibliography: ../../references.bib
---

Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) [@dm:dps] is a method for sampling from the posterior distribution in an inverse problem. To estimate the intractable likelihood term $p_t(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)$, with $\boldsymbol x \in \mathbb R^n$ and $\boldsymbol y \in \mathbb R^m$, DPS first factored the distribution by marginalizing over the clean data $\boldsymbol{x}_0$:
$$
p_t(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t) = \int p(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0) p_t(\boldsymbol{x}_0 \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t) d\boldsymbol{x}_0 = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0 \sim p_t(\boldsymbol{x}_0 \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)} \left[ p(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0) \right].
$$ {#eq-1}
This indicates that the likelihood of observing $\boldsymbol{y}$ given a noisy image $\boldsymbol{x}_t$ is the expected value of the clean data likelihood, weighted by the posterior $p_t(\boldsymbol{x}_0 \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)$. Because evaluating this expectation directly is intractable in practice, DPS proposed approximating it using the likelihood of the expected clean image:
$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol x_t} p_t(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t) \simeq \nabla_{\boldsymbol x_t} p_t(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\hat{x}}_0),
$$ {#eq-2}
where $\boldsymbol{\hat{x}}_0 \in \mathbb R^n$ is the posterior mean estimator computed via Tweedie's formula:
$$
\boldsymbol{\hat{x}}_0 = \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{x}_0 \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t].
$$ {#eq-3}

Geometrically, the score function $\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^n$ points in the direction orthogonal to the data manifold, pulling the sample toward the prior. Therefore, the model only addresses the direction which is normal to the data manifold, not being able to distinguish candidates to the solution along the manifold. In this context, Manifold Constrained Gradient (MCG) [@dm:mcg] showed that the likelihood term points in the direction tangent to the data manifold, correcting the trajectory of the score model during the reverse diffusion process. Furthermore, by MCG, the DPS approximation does not leave the data manifold.

The specific form of the likelihood depends on the distribution of the measurement noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \in \mathbb R^m$, but it can be written in general as:
$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}_t} \log p_t(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t) \simeq - \rho \nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}_t} \left\| \boldsymbol{y} - \mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{\hat{x}}_0) \right\|,
$$ {#eq-4}
where $\mathcal{A} : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^m$ is the forward operator of the inverse problem, $\| \cdot \| : \mathbb R^{m} \to \mathbb R_{\ge 0}$ is an appropriate norm matching the noise distribution and $\rho \in \mathbb R$ is a tunable step size. @alg:dps presents the overall DPS algorithm.

```pseudocode
#| label: alg:dps
#| html-indent-size: "1.2em"
#| html-line-number: true

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{DPS algorithm.}
\begin{algorithmic}
\REQUIRE Score network $\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$, measurement $\boldsymbol{y}$, forward operator $\mathcal{A}$, DPS step size $\rho$, noise schedule $\{t\}_{t=1}^{T}$, generic sampler $\text{Sampler}$

\STATE $\boldsymbol{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})$

\FOR{$t = T, \dots, 1$}
    \STATE $\boldsymbol{\hat{x}}_0 \gets \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}} \left( \boldsymbol{x}_t + (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t) \boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) \right)$

    \STATE $\boldsymbol{g}_{\text{DPS}} \gets \nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}_t} \left\| \boldsymbol{y} - \mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{\hat{x}}_0) \right\|_2_2$

    \STATE $\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \gets \text{Sampler}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, \boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, t) - \rho \boldsymbol{g}_{\text{DPS}}$
\ENDFOR

\RETURN $\boldsymbol{x}_0$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```
